result.summary: After winning at Chalcis, Hesiod goes to Delphi, receives an oracle warning him about Nemean Zeus, and is killed at Oenoe; his body is later moved to Orchomenus. Homer, defeated, wanders reciting poems, composes Midas's epitaph, dedicates a bowl at Delphi, and visits Athens, Corinth and Argos.

scenes.title: Hesiod's tripod and the oracle
scenes.summary: Hesiod dedicates his tripod and goes to Delphi, where the prophetess blesses him but warns him against the grove of Nemean Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Hesiod's life: the oracle foretells his death at Nemean Zeus's grove.

scenes.title: Hesiod's death at Oenoe
scenes.summary: Hesiod stays at Oenoe, is killed by his hosts' sons on suspicion of seducing their sister, and is washed ashore by dolphins. The killers are punished; another version names different brothers.
scenes.stakes: Hesiod's life and the killers' safety from their countrymen's anger.

scenes.title: Hesiod's tomb at Orchomenus
scenes.summary: The Orchomenians move Hesiod's body by oracle and inscribe his tomb.

scenes.title: Homer wanders and honours Midas
scenes.summary: Homer recites epics, writes Midas's epitaph for Xanthus and Gorgus, dedicates a silver bowl at Delphi, and composes the Odyssey.
scenes.stakes: Homer's renown, which he asks Apollo to grant.

scenes.title: Homer at Athens, Corinth, Argos
scenes.summary: Homer is entertained by Medon, improvises verses by the fire, is honoured at Corinth, and recites the Argive catalogue at Argos.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo used in Homer's dedication.
Zeus worshipped at a place called Nemea; the oracle's wording is ambiguous.

notable_quotes.reason: The ambiguous oracle warning Hesiod of death at Nemean Zeus's grove.
Famous epitaph of Midas, the enduring-forever tomb inscription.

analysis.text: The oracle's ambiguity shows the classic theme that fate is fulfilled precisely through attempts to avoid it.
The biographical traditions about Homer and Hesiod, with competing sources cited, show how Greeks built lives for poets from their verses and inscriptions.

legacy.text: The Midas epitaph was widely quoted in antiquity, including in Plato's Phaedrus, as an example of verse on a tomb.

fun_facts.text: The epitaph of Midas also appears in Plato's Phaedrus, where it is criticised for having lines that can be reordered without changing the sense.

language_notes.text: A tripod is a three-legged bronze cauldron, given as a prize or offering to a god. Helicon is the mountain sacred to the Muses.
The prophetess is the Pythia, the priestess of Apollo at Delphi, who spoke the god's oracles while inspired.
The oracle is ambiguous: Hesiod takes 'Nemean Zeus' to mean Nemea in the Peloponnesus, but a place in Locris bore the same name.
Ariadne, daughter of Minos of Crete, was loved by Theseus and Dionysus; local festivals honoured her in various places.
Alcidamas was a fourth-century BC rhetorician; his 'Museum' is the work on which this account of the contest draws.
'Gods of hospitality' refers to Zeus Xenios, protector of guests; the brothers had violated host-guest duty by killing Hesiod.
"As they were directed by an oracle": the Orchomenians consulted a god's oracle, which told them to move the bones, a common cause of hero-cult reburials.
Minyans: an old people associated with Orchomenus in Boeotia; "horse-driving" is a stock epithet for them.
"Judged by the test of wit" means measured by skill and wisdom, as in poetic contests.
The Thebais and Epigoni belong to the Theban cycle about the war of the Seven against Thebes and their sons' later attack; ancient writers doubted Homer wrote them.
Phoebus is a title of Apollo, meaning "bright"; Delphi was his chief oracle.
"Drew off" means he improvised or produced the lines on the spot.
The Son of Cronos is Jove (the Greek Zeus), here sending winter snow.
This is a passage from the Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad (Book 2), listing the Argive contingent.
"Linen jerkins" are linen body armour; "goads" are prods for driving animals.

context_notes.text: Delphi was the chief oracle of Apollo. Visitors consulted it and offered first fruits, a share of their gains, to the god.
Eratosthenes was a Hellenistic scholar and poet of Alexandria, known for measuring the Earth. He wrote a work on Hesiod.
Midas was the legendary king of Phrygia. The tomb figure of a weeping maiden is a funerary statue.
Medon was traditionally an early ruler of Athens, son of Codrus, after whom the Athenian archons were sometimes called Medontids.

literary_notes.text: Hesiod's fame is compared to the spreading light of dawn, suggesting it will reach everywhere and be lasting.
The prophecy of death in a grove of Nemean Zeus hints at the coming murder.
By avoiding the Peloponnesian Nemea, Hesiod walks straight into the fate foretold, so the oracle is fulfilled by his attempt to escape it.
A brisk, formulaic closing phrase moves the compiler's story from Hesiod to Homer.
The bronze maiden speaks in the first person, giving the tomb a voice.
The epitaph promises the statue will speak as long as nature lasts, stressing the monument's endlessness.
Children are called a crown and towers, and horses and ships ornaments, comparing things to what they honour or protect.
